To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

(i) the distribution of the segregating sites in the population of the strong-migration model converges to that in a panmictically mating population and (ii) in the case of two sequences, the distribution of the sites converges to that of a two-locus panmictically breeding model with recombination.

(1) the distribution of the segregating sites is the same for a panmicitic population and for a population in the strong-migration regime and (2) for a geographically structured, but well-mixed population the distribution of the numbers of segregating sites depends on the dimension of the torus, but not on the number of individuals.
the distribution of the segregating sites is asymptotically normal and the mean and variance are given in Theorem 2.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the effect of the population structure on the distribution of the segregating sites in the sample.
the distribution of the total number of segregating nucleotide sites among randomly chosen DNA sequences from a population with migration.
the number of segregation sites in DNA sequence data from geographically structured populations.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
the distribution of segregating sites converges to that of a panmictically mating population as migration becomes strong.

the distribution of segregating sites converges to that of a panmictically evolving population, as long as the number of sites is not too small, and as long as the migration rate is not too low, and that the distribution of the total number of segregating mutations in a sample of sequences from a geographi cally structured population is not affected by migration.
, as the number of individuals in the population increases, the distribution of the segregating sites converges to the distribution in a panmictically mating population.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
the number of segreging sites is not affected by the population structure.
, in the strong-migration and the weak-migration limits, the distribution of the segregating sites is the same as that in a panmictically evolving population.
the number of segreging sites is asymptotically normal, and that the variance converges to a constant as the population size increases.
The main takeaway from our work is that

the distribution of the segregating sites is determined by the migration rate, the population size, and the dimension of the torus, but not by the population density or by the spatial pattern of the population.

the distribution of the segregating sites in the two-sequence case can be approximated by that for a panmic population with the effective population size equal to the product of the sample size and the population size.
the distribution of the segregating sites is not affected by the population structure as long as there is enough migration.
